teile.einleitung: Carbohydrates are natural substances such as sugar, starch and cellulose that consist mainly of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Plants make them with the help of sunlight, and for us humans they are the most important source of energy in bread, pasta, rice and potatoes.
wichtigste: The name carbohydrates comes from the fact that many have the formula Cn(H2O)m, as if they were hydrates of carbon.
A distinction is made between simple sugars, double sugars and complex sugars.
Fructose is a ketohexose, glucose an aldohexose.
In water, glucose mostly forms a six-membered ring, the pyranose.
Cellulose and amylose both consist of glucose, but linked in different ways.
Chitin forms the outer skeleton of insects and crustaceans.
A brick-red precipitate in Fehling’s test shows a reducing sugar.

abschnitte.text: **Carbohydrates** are a large group of natural substances. Many of them have the formula Cn(H2O)m, which in the past made it look as if they were made of carbon and water. This is where the name comes from. Carbohydrates include sweet sugars as well as tasteless substances such as starch and cellulose.

**Monosaccharides** or simple sugars are the smallest building blocks, for example glucose (grape sugar) and fructose (fruit sugar). Glucose has an aldehyde group and is an aldohexose; fructose has a keto group and is a ketohexose. If two simple sugars join, a disaccharide is formed, such as table sugar, sucrose, or milk sugar, lactose. Long chains of many building blocks are called **polysaccharides**.

In water, glucose usually closes up into a ring. Mostly a six-membered ring of five carbon atoms and one oxygen atom is formed, the **pyranose**. When the ring closes, a new stereocentre is created, the anomeric carbon atom. Depending on how the OH group sits on it, it is called alpha or beta glucose.

Plants store energy as **starch**, which consists of amylose and amylopectin. Amylose is an unbranched chain with alpha-1,4 bonds; amylopectin is branched by extra alpha-1,6 bonds. Cellulose forms the cell walls of plants and is built from glucose with beta-1,4 bonds, which our body cannot split. The nitrogen-containing polysaccharide chitin makes the shells of insects and crustaceans hard.

**Fehling’s test** is used to check whether a sugar is reducing. The sample is heated with a deep blue copper solution. If a brick-red precipitate of copper(I) oxide forms, a reducing sugar such as glucose is present. Starch, on the other hand, is detected with iodine solution, which turns bluish black.

Carbohydrates provide about 17 kilojoules per gram and are the most important fuel for muscles and brain. During digestion, the body breaks starch down into glucose, which travels in the blood to the cells. The body stores surplus glucose as glycogen in the liver and muscles. In Switzerland sugar is obtained from sugar beet, which is processed in Aarberg and Frauenfeld.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simple sugar, the smallest building block of carbohydrates, for example glucose.
A complex sugar made of long chains of sugar units, such as starch.
A link between two sugar units.
The process in which plants use sunlight to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water.

gewusst: Cellulose is the most common organic substance on Earth.
Cows and other ruminants can only digest cellulose thanks to microorganisms in their rumen.
If you chew bread for a long time, it tastes sweeter, because an enzyme in saliva splits starch into sugar.

teile.einleitung: Carbon dioxide, CO2 for short, is a colourless and odourless gas made of carbon and oxygen. We breathe it out with every breath, and plants need it to grow. In too large amounts in the air, however, it strengthens the greenhouse effect and warms the climate.
wichtigste: A CO2 molecule consists of one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
Carbon dioxide is detected by bubbling it through limewater, which then turns cloudy.
Solid carbon dioxide is called dry ice and turns directly into gas at about minus 78 °C.
Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and collects near the ground, for example in fermentation cellars.
Because it pushes away oxygen, it is suitable for putting out fires.
Dissolved in water, it forms carbonic acid.
Yeast and baking powder make dough rise with carbon dioxide.

abschnitte.text: Carbon dioxide is a natural part of the air; its share is about 0.04 per cent (as of 2025). It is produced when people and animals breathe and when wood, coal, oil or gas burn. Plants take it in during **photosynthesis** and use it with the help of sunlight to make sugar. In doing so they give off oxygen, which we need to breathe.

Carbon dioxide is about one and a half times as heavy as air. That is why you can pour it like water from one glass into another and use it to put out a candle. In a school experiment, it is recognised with **limewater**, which turns milky. It can only be liquefied under increased pressure, which is why it is stored in pressurised cylinders.

At about minus 78 °C carbon dioxide becomes solid and is then called **dry ice**. It does not melt but turns directly into gas; this is called **sublimation**. That is why nothing wet is left behind. Dry ice is used for cooling goods and for fog effects on stage.

In fermentation cellars, a lot of carbon dioxide is produced when wine ferments, and it collects near the floor. Because you can neither see nor smell it, you can suffocate in it. Winemakers therefore use a burning candle to check whether there is enough oxygen. You also have to be careful when handling dry ice in closed rooms.

Carbon dioxide is a **greenhouse gas**: it lets sunlight through but holds back part of the Earth’s heat. Since the beginning of industrialisation its share in the air has risen sharply, mainly through burning coal, oil and natural gas. As a result the Earth is warming, and in Switzerland the glaciers are melting. Many countries, including Switzerland, therefore want to cut their CO2 emissions sharply.

In yeast dough, yeast produces carbon dioxide, which makes the dough rise; baking powder does the same without yeast. Fire extinguishers with CO2 are well suited for electrical equipment because they leave no residue. In drinks, the gas provides the fizz. The Zurich company **Climeworks** has developed plants that filter carbon dioxide directly out of the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that holds back heat and so warms the Earth.
The process in which plants make sugar and oxygen from CO2, water and light.
Solid carbon dioxide, very cold.
Changing directly from solid to gas.
A solution used to detect carbon dioxide, because it turns cloudy.

gewusst: An adult breathes out about one kilogram of carbon dioxide a day.
The Scot Joseph Black discovered the gas around 1750 and called it “fixed air”.
On Venus the atmosphere consists almost entirely of carbon dioxide, which is why it is over 400 °C hot there.

teile.einleitung: A condensation reaction is a chemical reaction in which two molecules join to form a larger molecule. A small molecule is split off, usually water. This is how proteins are made in our body, but also plastics such as nylon and PET.
wichtigste: In a condensation reaction two molecules join, and a small molecule such as water is split off.
When two amino acids condense, a peptide bond is formed.
Three amino acids give a tripeptide, and two water molecules are split off.
Two glucose molecules form the double sugar maltose via an alpha-1,4 bond.
The reverse of condensation is called hydrolysis.
The plastic nylon is made by polycondensation.
PET is made from terephthalic acid and ethanediol.

abschnitte.text: In a **condensation reaction**, two molecules react with each other and are linked by a new bond. A small molecule is left over, usually water, sometimes also hydrogen chloride or methanol. The name has nothing to do with steam condensing, but recalls that molecules are “compressed” together. Typically, reactive groups such as OH, COOH or NH₂ groups are involved.

In our cells, amino acids are linked into proteins by condensation. The bond between two amino acids is called a **peptide bond**. For each new bond, one water molecule is split off, so with three amino acids there are two. Sugars also join in this way: two glucose molecules form malt sugar, **maltose**, via an alpha-1,4 bond.

The reverse of a condensation is **hydrolysis**. A bond is split again with the help of water. During digestion, enzymes break down the proteins, fats and starch from food into small building blocks by hydrolysis. The body can take these into the blood and build new substances from them.

If both starting substances have two reactive groups, many molecules can join together into long chains. This **polycondensation** produces important plastics. Nylon, a polyamide, was developed in the USA in the 1930s and is used for stockings, ropes and toothbrush bristles. PET is made from terephthalic acid and ethanediol and is made into drinks bottles and textile fibres.

If you heat ethanol with concentrated sulphuric acid to about 140 °C, two ethanol molecules condense to form **diethyl ether**. When a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, an ester is formed with the loss of water; many esters smell of fruit. Silicones and some resins are also made by condensation reactions. So chemistry uses this principle in many different ways.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bond between two amino acids in a protein.
Splitting a bond with water, the opposite of condensation.
Condensation of many molecules into long chains, for example in plastics.
A substance made from an acid and an alcohol, which often smells fruity.

gewusst: A single PET chain can consist of hundreds of building blocks.
When a protein of 100 amino acids is built, 99 water molecules are split off.
In the 19th century diethyl ether was one of the first anaesthetics used in operations.

teile.einleitung: The carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer is the most important buffer system in our blood. It makes sure that the pH of the blood always stays almost the same, even when acids are produced during sport or after eating.
wichtigste: The normal value for arterial blood is between pH 7.35 and 7.45.
The buffer consists of carbonic acid, or dissolved CO₂, and hydrogen carbonate ions.
The enzyme carbonic anhydrase speeds up the reaction of CO₂ with water to form carbonic acid.
At pH 7.4, hydrogen carbonate and dissolved CO₂ are in a ratio of about 20 to 1.
The buffer works so well because it is an open system: CO₂ is breathed out through the lungs.
The kidneys regulate the hydrogen carbonate concentration in the long term.
Severe hyperventilation leads to respiratory alkalosis.

abschnitte.text: A **buffer** is a solution whose pH hardly changes when a little acid or base is added. It consists of a weak acid and its matching base. In the blood these are carbonic acid and the **hydrogen carbonate** ion HCO₃⁻, also called bicarbonate. If acid is added, hydrogen carbonate mops up the hydrogen ions; if base is added, carbonic acid releases hydrogen ions.

Carbon dioxide reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which breaks down into hydrogen ions and hydrogen carbonate. Without help, this step is fairly slow. The enzyme **carbonic anhydrase**, which is found mainly in the red blood cells, speeds it up enormously. The pKa of this system is about 6.1; at pH 7.4 this gives a ratio of about 20 parts hydrogen carbonate to one part dissolved CO₂.

Actually, the pKa of 6.1 is a long way from the blood pH of 7.4. Even so, the system buffers very well because it is an **open system**. The lungs can quickly breathe out excess CO₂, within minutes. The kidneys help more slowly but lastingly, by keeping back or getting rid of hydrogen carbonate and releasing acids in the urine.

If the pH falls below 7.35, this is called **acidosis**; if it rises above 7.45, alkalosis. Anyone who breathes very fast and deeply, that is hyperventilates, breathes out too much CO₂, and respiratory alkalosis results. In metabolic acidosis, for example in diabetic ketoacidosis, the body does the opposite and breathes more deeply and faster to get rid of CO₂. In this way it makes up for the excess acid in the short term.

Seawater also contains carbonic acid, hydrogen carbonate and carbonate. The oceans take up a large part of the CO₂ released by humans from the air. As a result, the pH of seawater falls; this is called **ocean acidification**. It then becomes harder for corals, mussels and snails to build their shells and skeletons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that shows how acidic or alkaline a solution is; 7 is neutral.
A solution that keeps its pH almost constant even when acid or base is added.
The ion HCO₃⁻, also called bicarbonate, which can mop up acid in the blood.
A condition in which the blood is too acidic.
A protein that speeds up chemical reactions in the body.

gewusst: Even small deviations of the blood pH of a few tenths can be life-threatening.
Carbonic anhydrase is one of the fastest enzymes known.
Many Swiss mineral waters contain hydrogen carbonate, which is given on the label.

teile.einleitung: Condensation is the change of a substance from the gas state to the liquid state. The best-known example is water vapour that cools down and turns back into drops of water. This is how clouds, fog, dew and the wet windows on a cold morning form.
wichtigste: Condensation is the change from gas to liquid.
It happens when a gas cools down or is compressed.
Clouds consist of tiny drops of water and ice that have formed by condensation.
The drops that form on the grass early in the morning are called dew.
Water from the air settles on a glass containing an ice-cold drink.
Vapour trails behind aeroplanes form from the water vapour in the exhaust.
Heat is released during condensation.

abschnitte.text: Most substances can be solid, liquid or gas. If a gas is cooled so much that its particles slow down and cling together again, it becomes liquid. This process is called **condensation**. Its opposite is boiling or evaporation. The air around us also always contains invisible water vapour, which can condense.

Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. If moist air cools down, at some point it reaches the **dew point**, the temperature at which it cannot hold any more water vapour. Then the water condenses on cold surfaces or on tiny dust particles in the air. By the way, condensation releases the heat that was needed earlier for evaporation.

**Clouds** and fog form when moist air cools down, for example because it has to rise over a mountain. Then billions of tiny water droplets form, and at great heights ice crystals. On clear nights the ground cools down a lot, and in the morning **dew** glitters on the grass. In autumn, fog often lies over the Swiss Plateau for weeks while it is sunny in the mountains.

A glass containing an ice-cold drink gets wet on the outside because water vapour from the air condenses on the cold glass. If you come into a warm house in winter, your glasses steam up because the warm, moist air cools down on the cold lenses. For the same reason, the inside of the window panes is often wet on cold mornings. The bathroom mirror also steams up after a shower.

High up, aeroplanes draw **vapour trails** across the sky. They form because the water vapour from the hot engine exhaust condenses and freezes immediately in the ice-cold air. Air conditioners cool the air, and moisture condenses, dripping out of a hose as water. In fridges and heat pumps, a refrigerant is evaporated and condensed in turn to move heat.

begriffe.erklaerung: The state of a substance: solid, liquid or gas.
Water in gas form, which you cannot see.
The temperature at which moist air starts to release water.
Changing from liquid to gas below the boiling point.

gewusst: The white “steam” above a saucepan is actually already condensed water in tiny droplets.
In the Atacama Desert, people catch fog with large nets to obtain drinking water.
Without condensation there would be no rain and no snow.

teile.einleitung: Carbon is a chemical element with the symbol C and the atomic number 6. It is the building block of all life, because every plant, every animal and every person consists largely of carbon compounds. It can look as different as a black pencil and a sparkling diamond.
wichtigste: Carbon has the symbol C and the atomic number 6.
Diamond and graphite both consist of pure carbon.
The lead of a pencil consists mainly of graphite and clay.
When carbon burns completely, carbon dioxide is formed.
Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds.
All living things are built from carbon compounds.

abschnitte.text: Carbon is in sixth place in the **periodic table**, so its nucleus has 6 protons. A carbon atom can form four bonds with other atoms. That is why it can form long chains, rings and huge molecules. No other element has so many different **compounds**, namely many millions.

Diamond is the hardest natural substance and consists of pure carbon in which every atom is firmly bonded to four neighbours. **Graphite** is also pure carbon, but the atoms lie in thin layers that slide easily over one another. That is why graphite is soft and black. Such different forms of an element are called **allotropes**.

The lead of a pencil is not made of lead but of **graphite** and clay. Charcoal for barbecues is almost pure carbon. Soot from a candle flame is also carbon. Steel contains a little carbon, which makes it harder than pure iron.

When carbon burns with enough oxygen, the gas **carbon dioxide** CO₂ is formed. If there is too little oxygen, poisonous carbon monoxide forms. Burning coal, oil and natural gas releases a lot of CO₂ into the air and strengthens the **greenhouse effect**. Plants take in CO₂ and use it with the help of sunlight to make sugar.

Proteins, fats, sugars and the genetic material DNA are all **carbon compounds**. The branch of chemistry that deals with them is called **organic chemistry**. With radioactive carbon-14, researchers can find out how old bones or wood are. This method is called radiocarbon dating and has also been used on finds from Swiss lake dwelling settlements.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic substance that consists of only one kind of atom.
A soft, black form of carbon from which pencil leads are made.
One of several forms in which an element can occur.
An invisible gas produced when things burn and when we breathe out.

gewusst: Almost a fifth of a person’s body weight is carbon.
Diamonds burn in air at very high temperatures because they are made of carbon.
Graphene, a layer of carbon only one atom thick, is one of the strongest materials known.

teile.einleitung: Carbonic acid forms when the gas carbon dioxide dissolves in water. In everyday life we usually mean the fizzy bubbles in sparkling mineral water and soft drinks. Chemically, carbonic acid is a weak acid that very easily breaks down again into water and gas.
wichtigste: The bubbles in sparkling mineral water consist of carbon dioxide.
Carbonic acid forms when carbon dioxide reacts with water.
Carbon dioxide stays dissolved longer in cold water than in warm water.
When you open a bottle of fizzy water, you hear a hiss because gas escapes.
If a bottle is left open for a long time, the gas escapes and the water tastes flat.
Some springs are naturally fizzy.
With a soda maker you can make tap water fizzy at home.

abschnitte.text: When **carbon dioxide** dissolves in water, a small part of it reacts with the water to form carbonic acid with the formula H2CO3. Most of the gas, however, simply stays dissolved as CO2. Carbonic acid is a weak **acid** and tastes slightly sour. That is why sparkling water tingles on the tongue and tastes a little different from still water.

In mineral water, a lot of gas is pressed into the bottle under **pressure**. As long as the bottle is closed, the gas stays dissolved. When you open it, the pressure drops, it hisses, and bubbles rise. Cold water can hold more gas than warm water, which is why warm sparkling water loses its fizz faster.

If you shake a bottle of fizzy water, many tiny gas bubbles form in the water. When you open it, they grow in a flash and carry the water upwards with them. That is why the contents spray out. If you wait a few minutes after shaking, the bubbles rise to the top and the bottle can be opened more calmly.

Deep in the Earth, carbon dioxide from the rock can get into the groundwater. When this water comes to the surface, it fizzes by itself; such springs are called **carbonated springs**. In Switzerland there are such springs, for example, in Scuol in the Lower Engadine. Most mineral waters in the shops, however, only get their fizz when they are bottled.

abschnitte.titel: A man from Geneva invents fizzy water
abschnitte.text: In the 18th century the Englishman Joseph Priestley showed how to add carbon dioxide to water. In 1783 the German-born watchmaker **Johann Jacob Schweppe** developed a process in Geneva for producing sparkling water in large quantities. This gave rise to the drinks brand Schweppes, which is still well known today. Today anyone can make sparkling water at home with a **soda maker**.

The sea also takes up carbon dioxide from the air, and carbonic acid forms. If the carbon dioxide content of the air rises, seawater becomes slightly more acidic; this is called **acidification**. It makes it harder for corals and mussels to build their shells. Rainwater also always has a little carbonic acid dissolved in it, which slowly dissolves limestone.

begriffe.erklaerung: A weak acid that forms when carbon dioxide dissolves in water.
A colourless gas made of carbon and oxygen, CO2.
A spring whose water naturally contains carbon dioxide.
A device that presses carbon dioxide from a gas cylinder into tap water.

gewusst: Pure carbonic acid as a substance can hardly be bottled, because it breaks down almost immediately into water and carbon dioxide.
The drinks brand Schweppes has its origins in Geneva.
Milk, fruit juice and tea normally have no fizz.

teile.einleitung: Carbon monoxide is an invisible and odourless gas with the formula CO. It is produced when something burns with too little oxygen, and it is very poisonous. At the same time it is an important raw material in industry, for example in making iron.
wichtigste: Carbon monoxide has the chemical formula CO.
It is produced in burning when there is too little oxygen.
The gas is colourless and odourless, which is why you do not notice it.
In the body it binds to the red blood pigment, about 200 to 300 times more strongly than oxygen.
A CO alarm warns of the dangerous gas in homes.
When carbon monoxide burns with oxygen, carbon dioxide is formed.
In the blast furnace, carbon monoxide removes the oxygen from the iron ore.

abschnitte.text: A **carbon monoxide** molecule consists of one carbon atom and one oxygen atom. It is a colourless, odourless and tasteless gas that is a little lighter than air. It is flammable and burns with a blue flame to form carbon dioxide CO₂. So the difference from CO₂ is exactly one oxygen atom, but that makes a big difference.

Carbon monoxide is produced by **incomplete combustion**, that is when wood, coal, gas, petrol or heating oil burn with too little oxygen. Dangerous sources are badly adjusted gas boilers, blocked chimneys, charcoal barbecues indoors or engines running in garages. Cigarette smoke also contains carbon monoxide. In cars, the catalytic converter turns a large part of it into carbon dioxide.

In the blood, the red blood pigment **haemoglobin** carries oxygen to all the organs. Carbon monoxide binds about 200 to 300 times more strongly to haemoglobin than oxygen does and pushes it out. As a result the brain and heart get too little oxygen. The first signs are headaches, dizziness, nausea and tiredness; later you can lose consciousness.

Because you can neither see nor smell the gas, **CO alarms** make sense in rooms with fireplaces or gas appliances. Heating systems and chimneys should be checked regularly; in Switzerland this is done by the chimney sweep. If you suspect poisoning, you must immediately open the windows, leave the room and call the emergency number 144. In hospital, those affected are given pure oxygen, sometimes in a pressure chamber.

In the **blast furnace**, carbon monoxide is formed from coke and air. It reacts with the iron ore, removes its oxygen and so leaves liquid pig iron behind. Together with hydrogen, carbon monoxide forms synthesis gas, from which methanol and other chemicals are made. Chemistry also uses the gas to make acetic acid and plastics.

begriffe.erklaerung: Burning with too little oxygen, which produces poisonous CO.
The red blood pigment that carries oxygen in the blood.
A device that sounds an alarm when there is too much carbon monoxide in the air.
A huge furnace in which pig iron is obtained from iron ore.

gewusst: A smoke alarm does not detect carbon monoxide; you need a separate CO alarm for that.
Carbon monoxide also occurs in small amounts in space and helps astronomers map gas clouds.
In the past, the town gas used for cooking in many Swiss towns contained a lot of carbon monoxide.

teile.einleitung: A tin can is an airtight metal container in which food keeps for years. The food is heated in the sealed can so that all germs die. The can was invented over 200 years ago, and still today almost every store cupboard holds cans of beans, tomatoes or tuna.
wichtigste: Tin cans make food last a long time.
They are usually made of sheet steel with a thin layer of tin against rust.
The food is heated in the sealed can so that germs die.
In a sealed can, food often stays good for several years.
Cans without a ring pull are opened with a tin opener.
A lid bulging outwards means that the contents may have gone off.
Steel cans can be separated from aluminium cans with a magnet.

abschnitte.text: Food goes off because bacteria and moulds grow in it. In a tin can, the food is filled in, the can is sealed airtight and then heated strongly. The germs die; this is called **sterilising**. Because no new germs can get in, the contents often stay edible for several years.

Most tin cans are made of **tinplate**, that is thin sheet steel with a very thin layer of tin. The tin protects the iron from rust. Inside, many cans also have a layer of lacquer so that acidic foods do not attack the metal. Drinks cans, on the other hand, are often made of **aluminium**.

Around 1810 the French cook Nicolas Appert discovered that food that is heated and sealed airtight keeps for a long time; he used glass bottles. In the same year the Englishman Peter Durand patented the tin can as a container. At first it was mainly soldiers and sailors who ate from cans. Strangely, the **tin opener** was only invented decades later; before that, cans were opened with a hammer and chisel.

If the lid of a can bulges outwards, which is called **blowing**, gases have formed inside. This can mean that bacteria have survived and the contents have gone off. Such cans must not be eaten but thrown away. You should also not use badly dented or rusty cans.

Empty tin cans are rinsed briefly and taken to the collection point for scrap metal. With a **magnet** you can check whether a can is made of steel, because aluminium is not attracted. The collected metal is melted down and made into new steel. This saves a lot of energy and raw materials.

In 1886 a cannery was founded in Lenzburg in the Aargau, from which the well-known brand Hero grew. There, vegetables, fruit and jam were produced in cans and jars. In the past, canned food was particularly important because there were no fridges yet. Even today, the federal government recommends keeping an **emergency supply** of long-life food at home.

begriffe.erklaerung: Food that has been made to keep, in a can or a jar.
Killing all germs by strong heating.
Thin sheet steel with a protective layer of tin.
A can lid bulging outwards, a warning sign that the contents have gone off.

gewusst: The tin opener was only invented about 50 years after the tin can.
On polar expeditions, cans were found whose contents had still not gone off after many decades.
A tin can can be recycled again and again without the metal losing quality.

teile.einleitung: Hydrocarbons are chemical compounds that consist only of carbon and hydrogen. They are the main components of natural gas, crude oil, petrol and candle wax. Depending on the structure of their molecules, they are divided into families, for example alkanes, alkenes and aromatics.
wichtigste: Hydrocarbons consist only of carbon and hydrogen atoms.
Alkanes have only single bonds and the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Alkenes have at least one C=C double bond.
Methane is the main component of natural gas.
Benzene, with the formula C₆H₆, is the best-known aromatic compound.
Hydrocarbons are important fuels and raw materials for plastics.

abschnitte.text: Hydrocarbons contain only the elements C and H. The carbon atoms form chains or rings to which the **hydrogen atoms** are attached. Small molecules such as methane and propane are gases, medium ones such as octane are liquids and large ones such as paraffin wax are solid. The most important source is **crude oil**, which is separated into its components in refineries.

**Alkanes** have only single bonds and follow the formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. The first ones are called methane, ethane, propane and butane. The unbranched alkane with eight carbon atoms is called **octane**; it is an important part of petrol. Alkanes are rather unreactive, but in light they react with chlorine by **free radical substitution**.

**Alkenes** have at least one C=C double bond; the simplest is ethene C₂H₄. The double bond makes them reactive. If you add ethene to brown bromine water, it turns colourless because an **electrophilic addition** takes place. Alkynes such as ethyne even have a triple bond; ethyne is used in welding.

Benzene has the formula C₆H₆ and forms a ring of six carbon atoms. Its electrons are spread over the whole ring, which makes it particularly stable. Such substances are called **aromatics**, because many of them have a strong smell. Benzene is poisonous and causes cancer, which is why it is handled carefully in the laboratory.

**Methane** is the main component of natural gas, with which many houses in Switzerland are heated. Propane and butane are filled into gas bottles for barbecues and camping. The plastic polyethylene is made from ethene. Burning hydrocarbons produces CO₂, which strengthens **climate change**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A hydrocarbon with only single bonds, for example methane.
A hydrocarbon with at least one double bond between two carbon atoms.
A formula that shows how many atoms of each kind a molecule has.
A reaction in which particles attach to a double bond.

gewusst: Methane is also produced in the stomachs of cows and is released when they burp.
The octane number at the petrol station shows how resistant a petrol is to knocking.
On Saturn’s moon Titan there are whole lakes of liquid methane and ethane.

teile.einleitung: Corrosion is the slow destruction of a material, usually a metal, by chemical reactions with its surroundings. The best-known example is the brown rust on iron. Every year corrosion causes huge damage to cars, bridges and machines.
wichtigste: Simply put, rust consists of hydrated iron(III) oxide.
Iron rusts when water and oxygen are present at the same time.
A local cell is a short-circuited galvanic cell on a metal surface.
Salt solution conducts ions better, which is why cars rust faster on salted roads.
If two different metals touch in damp conditions, the less noble one corrodes more.
Aluminium resists corrosion thanks to a dense oxide layer.
Stainless steel contains at least about 10.5 per cent chromium.

abschnitte.text: The word **corrosion** comes from the Latin “corrodere”, which means to gnaw away. Metals react with oxygen, water, acids or salts from their surroundings. Base metals such as iron, zinc or aluminium corrode more easily than noble metals such as gold or platinum. Concrete and plastics can also be attacked, but in everyday life we usually mean metals.

Iron only rusts when **water** and **oxygen** come together. The iron gives up electrons and becomes iron ions, while the oxygen takes up the electrons. In the end **rust** is formed, simply put hydrated iron(III) oxide. Rust is loose and porous, which is why moisture can get deeper and deeper into the metal.

Often a metal surface acts like a tiny battery, a so-called **local cell**. If two different metals touch in a damp environment, the less noble metal is dissolved. A steel screw in an aluminium sheet therefore makes the aluminium corrode more. In tin-plated iron, tinplate, a scratch rusts particularly quickly because tin is more noble than iron.

Salt dissolves in water to form ions, which conduct electricity well. That is why cars rust faster on salted roads in winter, and seawater is also very aggressive. Warmth and acidic air, for example from exhaust gases, also speed up corrosion. In dry air, on the other hand, iron hardly rusts.

Aluminium is a base metal but hardly corrodes in everyday life. In air it immediately forms a very thin, dense **oxide layer** that protects the metal underneath. Stainless steel, which contains at least about 10.5 per cent chromium, works in a similar way. Against rust on ordinary iron, **hot-dip galvanising** helps, for example, in which steel parts are dipped into liquid zinc.

begriffe.erklaerung: A reddish brown, loose layer that forms when iron reacts with water and oxygen.
A metal that reacts easily with oxygen, for example iron or zinc.
A tiny, short-circuited battery on a metal surface that causes corrosion.
A thin layer of metal and oxygen on the surface of a metal.

gewusst: Rust takes up more space than the iron it came from and can even crack concrete.
Gold practically does not corrode, which is why gold treasures thousands of years old still shine today.
Corrosion damage costs industrial countries many billions of francs every year.

teile.einleitung: The squeaky pop test is a simple experiment used in chemistry lessons to detect hydrogen. You hold a test tube containing the gas to a flame and listen carefully: if it whistles or barks, there was oxyhydrogen in it.
wichtigste: Oxyhydrogen is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen.
Oxyhydrogen reacts most violently in a volume ratio of 2 to 1 of hydrogen to oxygen.
When oxyhydrogen reacts, water is formed.
For the test, you hold the test tube with the opening facing downwards.
A whistling or barking sound shows a positive test.
If there is almost pure hydrogen in the tube, you only hear a quiet “pop”.
In the school laboratory, hydrogen is often made from zinc and hydrochloric acid.

abschnitte.text: **Oxyhydrogen** is a mixture of hydrogen and oxygen. It can also form when hydrogen mixes with air, because air contains about 21 per cent oxygen. If a flame or a spark comes along, the two gases react with each other in a flash. Water is formed, and a great deal of energy is released, which causes the bang. The reaction is most violent with two parts hydrogen to one part oxygen.

First you collect the gas in a **test tube**. Because hydrogen is much lighter than air, you hold the tube with the opening facing downwards so that the gas does not escape. Then you quickly bring the opening to a burner flame. You always wear safety goggles, and the teacher shows exactly how it is done.

A whistling or barking sound means that there was a mixture of hydrogen and air in the tube. If, on the other hand, there is almost pure hydrogen in the tube, you only hear a quiet “pop”, and the gas burns away calmly. If everything stays silent, there was no hydrogen. After the test you sometimes see a fine film of water in the test tube, the product of the reaction.

In the school laboratory, hydrogen is usually obtained by pouring dilute **hydrochloric acid** over **zinc**. Hydrogen gas bubbles up and zinc chloride forms. Hydrogen can also be obtained by electrolysis, that is by splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen with electricity. The squeaky pop test then shows that hydrogen really has been produced.

Hydrogen can be dangerous if it mixes with air unnoticed. In 1937 the hydrogen-filled airship **“Hindenburg”** burnt as it was landing at Lakehurst in the USA. Since then, airships and balloons have been filled with non-flammable helium. Used in a controlled way, however, the reaction of hydrogen and oxygen provides valuable energy, for example in rocket engines and fuel cells.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of hydrogen and oxygen that reacts with a bang when ignited.
The lightest chemical element, a colourless, flammable gas.
An experiment used to check whether a particular substance is present.
Splitting a substance with the help of electricity.

gewusst: The exhaust of a hydrogen fuel cell is pure water.
Hydrogen is about 14 times lighter than air.
At about 245 metres long, the Hindenburg was one of the largest aircraft ever built.

teile.einleitung: Compost is dark, fertile soil that is made from garden and kitchen waste. Countless tiny creatures such as bacteria, fungi and earthworms break down leaves, grass cuttings and apple cores. In this way waste becomes food for new plants again.
wichtigste: A compost heap turns into fertile soil.
Apple cores, vegetable peelings and leaves belong on the compost.
Cooked meat does not belong on the garden compost.
Tiny fungi and bacteria break down the waste.
Earthworms help a great deal with composting.
It takes a few months for garden waste to turn into compost.
In Switzerland, garden and kitchen waste is collected as green waste.

abschnitte.text: Compost forms when plant waste rots in the air. In the end a crumbly, dark soil is left that smells like forest floor. This soil contains a lot of **humus** and nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Gardeners mix it into beds so that plants grow better.

Most of the work is done by **bacteria** and fungi that are so small that you cannot see them. After them come larger animals such as woodlice, springtails and above all **earthworms**. They eat the remains and leave behind nutrient-rich crumbs. All these creatures need air and moisture, so the compost should neither dry out nor get too wet.

When the tiny creatures are at work, heat is produced. Inside a large fresh compost heap it can get hotter than 60 °C. This heat kills many weed seeds and germs. After a few weeks the heap cools down, and mature **compost** slowly forms.

Fruit and vegetable scraps, coffee grounds, tea bags, eggshells, leaves, grass cuttings and small branches belong on the compost. Cooked food, meat and bones do not, because they attract rats and smell bad. Plastic, glass, metal and cat litter do not belong there either. A good compost is a **mixture** of moist and dry, coarse and fine waste.

Many municipalities in Switzerland collect **green waste** with a separate collection or have collection points. It is turned into compost in large composting plants. Part of it goes to **biogas plants**, where bacteria turn it into gas without oxygen. This biogas is used to produce electricity and heat, and the remains serve as fertiliser.

About a third of our household waste consists of scraps that can be composted. If they are composted, they do not end up in the waste incineration plant. The nutrients return to the soil, and less artificial fertiliser is needed. You also learn a lot about the **cycle** of nature from your own compost heap.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fertile soil made from rotted plant waste.
The dark, fertile part of the soil made of broken-down plant and animal remains.
Garden and kitchen waste that is collected separately in Switzerland.
A flammable gas that bacteria produce from waste without oxygen.
Living things that break down dead plants and animals.

gewusst: A handful of mature compost contains more tiny living things than there are people on Earth.
There are special worm bins in which compost worms can process kitchen waste even in a flat.
